title: Nvidia Discloses $21 Billion Stake in SpaceX as Tech Giants Reveal Musk Empire Holdings
excerpt: The chipmaker's SpaceX position, acquired through its early investment in xAI, makes it one of several major tech companies with significant exposure to Elon Musk's space and AI conglomerate.
body:
• Nvidia disclosed a $21 billion stake in SpaceX as of the end of Q2 2026, stemming from its early investment in xAI before the February merger
  • Alphabet revealed the largest tech stake at $94.1 billion, while Tesla holds $3 billion — putting combined Big Tech exposure to SpaceX well above $100 billion
  • SpaceX has committed to building AI infrastructure exclusively on Nvidia hardware, with plans to expand compute capacity from 2 GW to 10 GW by end of 2027
  • The disclosures come as SpaceX shares trade around $118, roughly 13% below their June IPO price of $135

Big Tech's SpaceX Bet Comes Into Focus

Nvidia has disclosed a $21 billion stake in SpaceX as of the end of the second quarter, according to financial filings reported by the Financial Times and Bloomberg. The chipmaker's position in Elon Musk's space and AI conglomerate stems from its early investment in xAI, the artificial intelligence company that merged with SpaceX in February 2026.

https://x.com/HIT/status/2088387774093148619

The disclosure places Nvidia among a growing roster of major technology companies with substantial exposure to SpaceX, which went public in June at $135 per share and now carries a market capitalization of roughly $2.2 trillion. Nvidia also holds approximately $30 billion in Intel shares, the result of a $5 billion strategic investment completed in late 2025.

Alphabet Leads the Pack

Google parent Alphabet disclosed the largest Big Tech stake in SpaceX, valued at approximately $94.1 billion as of the end of June — representing about 4% of SpaceX's market cap. The company said $80 billion of its holdings are subject to short-term restrictions on the ability to sell, with an additional $14.1 billion restricted through September 2027, according to SEC filings.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=vpxBRk75Cao

Tesla disclosed a more modest $3 billion stake, per its second-quarter earnings report. Together, the disclosed tech company holdings in SpaceX exceed $120 billion, underscoring how deeply intertwined Big Tech and Musk's empire have become.

"Going forward, we've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia, because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture."

— Elon Musk, SpaceX earnings call

A Symbiotic Relationship

The financial ties between Nvidia and SpaceX extend well beyond a passive equity stake. On SpaceX's second-quarter earnings call, Musk announced that the company would build its AI infrastructure exclusively on Nvidia chips going forward, citing the Vera Rubin architecture as superior to alternatives.

SpaceX directed approximately 86% of its $18.4 billion in second-quarter capital expenditure toward AI infrastructure, with plans to expand computing capacity from 2 gigawatts at the end of 2026 to 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027 — all on Nvidia hardware. The two companies also announced a partnership to design the Starmind AI1 satellite compute payload, which would place Nvidia's next-generation Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs in orbit.

SpaceX reported $7.8 billion in second-quarter revenue, beating analyst expectations of $6.93 billion. Starlink, its satellite internet division, brought in $4.29 billion, making it the most lucrative segment. The AI division contributed $2.56 billion.

Lock-Up Expirations Loom

The stake disclosures arrive at a sensitive moment for SpaceX shareholders. Shares have fallen roughly 13% from their IPO price to around $118, and a series of staggered lock-up expirations beginning August 6 could free early investors to trade their holdings.

For Nvidia, the SpaceX stake represents both a financial asset and a strategic partnership. The chipmaker has positioned itself as the indispensable supplier to SpaceX's sprawling AI ambitions, from ground-based data centers to an orbital computing constellation that some analysts view as speculative but potentially transformative.

The coming quarters will test whether these intertwined bets — financial and operational — deliver the returns that both companies and their investors are banking on.
